text: You now have three building blocks: the shift-left mindset, the threat-modeling practice for finding risks specific to your system, and the OWASP Top 10 vocabulary for naming common risk categories. This lesson ties them together by walking across the full Secure Software Development Lifecycle — the stage-by-stage map the rest of this course is organized around.

The traditional SDLC — plan, design, develop, test, deploy, operate — describes how software gets built regardless of security. The Secure SDLC overlays a security activity onto every one of those stages instead of appending one activity at the end. Plan defines security requirements alongside functional ones. Design threat models the architecture. Develop pairs secure coding with static analysis and peer review. Build and Test run SAST, dependency scanning, secrets detection, and IaC scanning. Release adds a final policy gate before a build ships. Deploy hardens the running environment with least-privilege identity and vaulted secrets. Operate keeps watching with monitoring, audit logging, and incident response.

Picture Northbridge Retail's checkout service moving through this. A requirement specifies payment data must never be logged in plaintext — that's Plan. The team threat models the payment flow and finds the trust boundary with the processor — that's Design. A developer uses a vetted payment SDK instead of handling card data directly, and the pipeline runs SAST, dependency, and secrets scans on every pull request — Develop and Build/Test. A policy gate blocks the deploy on any critical finding, the service runs under a scoped workload identity in a hardened container, and Azure Monitor logs every access to payment resources for the on-call rotation to review — Release, Deploy, and Operate.

Each stage's activity catches a different kind of problem — a threat model won't catch a leaked dependency vulnerability, and a dependency scan won't catch an architectural flaw with no code to point to. The SSDLC isn't a checklist completed once; every pull request restarts the cycle at Develop and Build/Test. Next up, Chapter 2: IAM principles and least privilege.
